Summary: US-01 PIN fast-switch between volunteers on a shared tablet
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer sharing a tablet with the rest of my shift, I can switch to my own account with a short PIN so that the line keeps moving while every action is still recorded under my name.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A volunteer already on shift at this site can take over the device with a 4-6 digit PIN instead of a full password.
* Switching accounts takes under five seconds and does not discard an entry the previous volunteer left open.
* PIN switching is offered only on devices registered to a site, never on a personal device.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case assumes one person per device and a full credential every time. It says nothing about the shared-tablet reality of a distribution table or about a fast re-identification method.

*Traceability*
Epic UC-01 · Story US-01 · MoSCoW: Must

Summary: US-02 Live view of volunteers signed in at my site
Description:
*User story*
As a site coordinator, I want to see who is signed in at my site right now so that I know the table is covered and can tell who recorded a transaction when a participant queries it later.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A roster panel lists the volunteers currently holding a session at the coordinator's site, with the time each signed in.
* The coordinator can sign a volunteer out remotely when a device is left unattended.
* The panel is visible to coordinators and Administrators only.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case writes a login audit entry but never surfaces who is currently active. Real-time visibility for the person running the shift is a separate need.

Summary: US-03 Confidentiality acknowledgement on first login
Description:
*User story*
As a new volunteer signing in for the first time, I want to read and acknowledge the confidentiality rules before I see any participant data so that I understand what I am responsible for.

*Acceptance criteria*
* First successful login presents the current confidentiality and data-handling statement before the home screen.
* The volunteer must acknowledge it to continue; declining ends the session without exposing participant data.
* The version acknowledged and the date are stored against the account.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case treats onboarding as something an Administrator records beforehand. It never puts the obligation in front of the volunteer at the moment they gain access.

Summary: US-04 Today's checked-in households at the top of search
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer with a queue forming, I want the people who have checked in for today's event to appear at the top of my search so that I am not typing full names while ten households wait.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Participants checked in at the current event appear first, marked with their check-in time.
* The list refreshes as further households check in, without the volunteer reloading the screen.
* Typing any criterion immediately reverts to a normal search across all participants.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case offers recent-participant browsing over the last 30 days but has no concept of a check-in queue for the event currently running.

Summary: US-05 Search and serve participants by preferred name
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer serving someone who does not go by their legal name, I can find them by the name they actually use so that I am not asking them to repeat their documents in front of a queue.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A participant record holds a preferred name in addition to the legal name.
* Search matches on either name and displays the preferred name first in results.
* Receipts and voucher paperwork use the preferred name where one is recorded.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case lists the searchable fields and never contemplates a preferred or chosen name, nor the dignity issue of asking someone to identify themselves by a name they do not use.

Summary: US-06 Accent-insensitive participant search
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer at a site serving many non-English-speaking households, I can find a participant whether or not I type the accents in their name so that a missing diacritic does not create a duplicate record.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Search treats accented and unaccented forms of a character as equivalent in both directions.
* The system warns at registration when a new name differs from an existing one only by accents.
* Sorting of results is not disturbed by the accent-insensitive matching.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case specifies partial and phonetic matching on surnames but is silent on diacritics, which is the commonest source of duplicate records at multilingual sites.

Summary: US-07 Applicant self-service pre-registration
Description:
*User story*
As an applicant waiting in line, I want to start my own registration on my phone or a kiosk tablet so that the volunteer only has to check my answers rather than key everything in.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A QR code at the site opens a self-entry form covering the non-verified fields.
* The volunteer sees the submission as a pending draft and completes verification, consent and proof of residence at the table.
* A draft not claimed within 24 hours is discarded and no participant record is created.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case has the volunteer keying every field during an interview. Self-service pre-entry, and the split between what an applicant may enter and what a volunteer must verify, appear nowhere in it.

Summary: US-08 Save an interrupted registration as a draft
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer interrupted part-way through an intake, I can save a registration as a draft and return to it so that an interruption does not cost the applicant their place in the queue.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A partly completed registration can be saved without passing validation.
* Drafts are listed on the volunteer's home screen with the applicant's name and how long ago they were saved.
* A draft is not a participant record: it cannot receive a distribution and is not searchable by other functions.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case runs registration as one uninterrupted transaction that either validates or fails. It never accounts for the interruptions that characterise a live distribution day.

Summary: US-09 Coordinator-configurable intake questions
Description:
*User story*
As a programme coordinator, I want to change the intake questions we ask without waiting for a developer so that the form matches what our current grant requires.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A coordinator can add, retire or reorder optional intake questions and mark them required or optional.
* Retiring a question preserves the answers already collected and stops it being asked.
* Changes take effect at the next intake without a release.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case fixes the intake fields in its flow of events. The fact that funders change their reporting demands mid-programme, and that the form must follow, is not addressed.

Summary: US-10 Participant self-service contact update
Description:
*User story*
As a participant who has moved house, I can update my address and phone number myself through a link so that I do not have to wait until the next distribution to correct them.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A participant can reach a self-service form through a link sent to their recorded contact method.
* Self-submitted changes to address are held for volunteer confirmation at the next visit; contact-number changes apply at once.
* The participant is told which changes took effect immediately and which are pending.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case gives amendment entirely to Volunteers and Administrators. Participant self-service, and the distinction between changes that need verification and those that do not, is new.

Summary: US-11 Prompt to reconfirm stale contact details
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer, I want to be prompted to confirm a household's contact details when they have not been checked for a year so that our outreach lists stay reachable.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A prompt appears at the table when the contact details were last confirmed more than a configurable period ago.
* Confirming without change records the confirmation date; the prompt can be deferred once per visit.
* The date of last confirmation is visible on the participant record.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case handles an amendment the user chooses to make. It never prompts for one, and has no notion of data going stale between visits.

Summary: US-12 Service-preference notes on the participant record
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer, I can record how a household prefers to be served — help carrying bags to the car, for instance — so that the next volunteer serves them the same way without them having to ask again.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A short service-note field is available on the participant record, visible at the table.
* Notes are limited to service preferences; the field carries guidance that health, financial and personal circumstances must not be recorded.
* The author and date of each note are shown and notes can be retired when no longer relevant.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case treats the participant record as identity and eligibility data only. Operational service preferences, and the boundary on what may be written in a free-text note, are not covered.

Summary: US-13 Picture-based size and type picker for mixed breeds
Description:
*User story*
As a volunteer recording a mixed-breed dog, I can choose from a picture-based size and type picker so that I record something useful when neither of us knows the breed.

*Acceptance criteria*
* The pet form offers a visual picker of size bands and common body types as an alternative to typing a breed.
* The selection populates the size band used for the allotment.
* Breed remains recordable as free text for participants who know it.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case assumes breed and weight are simply known and entered. It does not address the very common case of an uncertain mixed breed, where the allotment still depends on getting the size band right.

Summary: US-14 Vaccination expiry prompt at the table
Description:
*User story*
As a participant, I want to be told at the table when my dog's rabies vaccination is about to expire so that I can arrange it before it lapses.

*Acceptance criteria*
* The system flags pets whose recorded vaccination expires within a configurable window when the household is served.
* The volunteer is given the partner clinics offering low-cost vaccination to hand on.
* Pets with no recorded vaccination date are shown as unknown rather than as expired.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case captures the vaccination date as a stored field and stops there. Acting on it at the moment the household is in front of a volunteer is a distinct capability.

Summary: US-15 Flag pets that have outgrown their size band
Description:
*User story*
As a coordinator, I want to see which pets have grown into a different size band since their details were recorded so that a puppy that is now full-grown receives the right allotment.

*Acceptance criteria*
* The system lists pets whose recorded age implies a size band different from the one stored.
* A volunteer can confirm or correct the weight at the next visit from that list.
* No allotment changes automatically without a human confirming the weight.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case records age and weight once and recalculates the allotment from what is stored. That stored weight silently going out of date as an animal grows is not considered anywhere in it.

As a volunteer issuing food, I can scan the barcode on the bag rather than find the product in a list so that I record what I actually handed over instead of what looked closest on screen.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Scanning a product barcode selects the product and its unit weight.
* An unrecognised barcode can be associated with an existing product once and is then recognised at every site.
* Manual product selection remains available when a bag is unlabelled or the barcode is damaged.

*Adds beyond the use case*

Summary: US-17 Record a declined product and substitute within allotment
Description:
*User story*
As a participant whose cat will not eat one of the products offered, I can decline it and take more of another within my allotment so that nothing I carry home goes to waste.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A volunteer can record a declined product and the reason, and substitute within the same allotment and species.
* Declines are recorded distinctly from shortfalls, which are the pantry's fault rather than a preference.
* Repeat declines of the same product are visible on the household record so the offer changes next time.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case allows substitution only when stock runs short. Participant preference as a legitimate reason to substitute, and the value of recording it, do not appear.

Summary: US-18 Live event dashboard for the site coordinator
Description:

As a coordinator running the event, I want a live count of households served and stock remaining so that I can reduce allotments before we run out rather than after.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A coordinator view shows households served, pets served and remaining stock by product, updating as distributions are recorded.
* The view warns when projected demand from the households checked in exceeds remaining stock.

The use case handles one household at a time and reports the event afterwards. Managing the event while it is still running, from figures accumulating in real time, is absent.

As a participant, I can see my own distribution history on my phone so that I can check what I received without asking a volunteer to look it up for me.

Summary: US-20 Surface irregular visit patterns as a welfare prompt
Description:

As a volunteer, I want to see when a household's visits have become irregular so that I can ask whether they are having trouble getting to the site.

*Acceptance criteria*
* The history view marks a household whose interval between visits has lengthened materially against its own pattern.

* The prompt can be dismissed for a visit without recording anything about the household.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case presents history as a list and a set of totals. Interpreting the pattern for the volunteer, and doing so as a welfare prompt rather than a compliance flag, is new.

Summary: US-21 Clinic directions and hours from the voucher
Description:
*User story*
As a participant holding a voucher, I want the clinic's address, hours and directions on my phone so that I actually get there on the day.

*Acceptance criteria*
* The voucher carries a link or QR code opening the clinic's location, opening hours and telephone number.
* The information is available without an account and works on a low-end phone.
* A printed voucher carries the same details in text so a phone is not required.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case produces a voucher and clinic instructions but never says what they contain or how they are read. That they should be interactive, account-free and usable on a low-end phone — the practical journey where funded surgeries are actually lost — is nowhere in it.

* Declines are distinguished from shortfalls and from products that were simply out of stock.
* The report can be filtered by species and by site.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case reports quantities issued and shortfalls. Declines — the participant refusing a product — do not exist in it, and they are exactly what should change what the pantry accepts.

Summary: US-38 Wait-time reporting by site and shift
Description:
*User story*
As a coordinator, I want to see how long households wait at each site so that I can put more volunteers on the shifts where the queue is worst.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Wait time is derived from check-in to distribution and reported by site, day and hour.
* The report shows the number of volunteers on shift alongside the wait so the two can be compared.
* Households that leave without being served are counted separately.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case reports on who is enrolled and who has lapsed. The service experience — how long people stand in line, and whether staffing matches demand — is not among its variants.

Summary: US-39 Report households referred out of the service area
Description:
*User story*
As the director, I want to know how many households we turned away for living outside our service area so that I can make the case to funders for widening the boundary.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Applicants recorded as referred out are reportable by period and by postal code.
* The report shows the pantry each applicant was referred to, where recorded.
* Figures are aggregate and subject to the same small-cell suppression as other participant reports.

*Adds beyond the use case*
Registration records an applicant as referred out when they fall outside the service area, but no reporting use case ever counts them. Unmet demand is invisible in the specification as it stands.

Summary: US-40 Estimate of litters prevented
Description:
*User story*
As the director, I want our referrals expressed as an estimate of litters prevented so that our impact is stated in terms funders respond to rather than as a count of vouchers.

*Acceptance criteria*
* An estimate is derived from completed surgeries using a published, cited multiplier that an Administrator can update.
* The report states the multiplier, its source and that the figure is an estimate.
* The underlying count of completed surgeries is always shown alongside the estimate.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case reports completions, spend and time to surgery — all operational measures. Translating them into the outcome language funders use, with the honesty caveats that requires, is new.

Summary: US-41 Compare spay/neuter uptake between our own sites
Description:
*User story*
As a coordinator, I want to compare spay and neuter uptake between our sites so that I can find out what the site with the highest uptake is doing differently.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Referral offers, acceptances and completions are reported per site as rates, not raw counts.
* Sites with too few referrals for a meaningful rate are marked rather than ranked.
* The report can be broken down by species and by the volunteer making the offer.

*Adds beyond the use case*
The use case compares clinics, which are external providers. Comparing the pantry's own sites — where the conversation with the participant actually happens — is not one of its variants.
